earliest_print_source: Way of the Peaceful Warrior, Dan Millman, 1980 (widely cited to this book; page/edition unverified)
notes: I recall this line as spoken by the 'Socrates' character in Millman's Way of the Peaceful Warrior (1980), usually quoted as 'Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't really live at all.' The attribution to Millman is consistent everywhere I have seen it and the voice matches the book. I cannot confirm the exact page or edition from memory, so I am holding this below the primary-source band.

Circulates widely and consistently under Dan Millman's name, but I cannot place it in any specific book of his. The sentiment is close to his 'peaceful warrior' material, which makes the attribution plausible rather than evidenced. No primary source known to me.

Reads like Millman's prose and likely comes from Everyday Enlightenment: The Twelve Gateways to Personal Growth (1998), which contains a gateway on managing finances framed around sufficiency rather than wealth or poverty. I cannot confirm the passage, so I am not asserting that book as the source.

This passage is consistently attributed to Dave Ramsey and matches his voice and his standard theme that money behavior reveals character. It most likely comes from The Total Money Makeover or the Financial Peace material, but I cannot pin the book or page, so no print source is asserted. Attribution is strong; the citation is not.

Standardly attributed to broadcaster David Brinkley (usually as 'A successful man is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks others have thrown at him'), but I know of no speech, broadcast, or book of his where it originates. Variants of the 'foundation from thrown bricks' aphorism circulated in American inspirational writing before Brinkley's prominence, which makes him a plausible popularizer rather than a confirmed author. The text here has also been gender-neutralized from the common form.

earliest_print_source: The Philosophy of Despair, David Starr Jordan, 1902 (widely cited; exact page unverified)
notes: Genuine David Starr Jordan, the Stanford naturalist and first president of the university. The original reads 'The world turns aside to let any man pass who knows whither he is going' and is commonly cited to his 1902 essay The Philosophy of Despair. The corpus records the author as 'David S. Jordan'; the standard form of the name is David Starr Jordan. The quote text here has been gender-neutralized from the original.
suggested_reattribution: David Starr Jordan (name normalization, same person)

notes: Attributed to David J. Schwartz and generally traced to The Magic of Thinking Big (1959), whose chapter on goals argues exactly this. The attribution is consistent and the source book is very likely correct, but I cannot verify the wording or page from memory, so I am leaving the print citation blank rather than asserting it. Note the corpus records the author as 'David Schwartz'; the usual byline is David J. Schwartz.

Attributed to singer Debby Boone across quote compilations, with no primary source I can identify — no book, interview, or speech. The attribution is uniform but rests entirely on quote-site repetition, which is weak evidence.

A signature Dee Hock line, from the Visa founder's chaordic-organization material. It was widely circulated after the 1996 Fast Company profile of Hock and appears in the same vein as Birth of the Chaordic Age (1999). Attribution to Hock is strong and consistent; I cannot confirm which of the two is the earliest print appearance, so I am not asserting a citation.

Chopra's vocabulary — 'conscious choice-maker' and actions that are 'evolutionary' are his terms from the Law of Karma chapter of The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success (1994). Attribution to Chopra is solid; I cannot confirm this exact sentence, so it may be a condensation of the passage rather than a verbatim line.

Widely quoted as Chopra and consistent with his teaching on non-resistance, but I cannot place it in any of his books or talks. Short aphorisms like this one attach easily to famous teachers, so I am keeping this well below the promotion bar.

earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Least Effort chapter (locus from memory, page unverified)
notes: This is the acceptance component of the Law of Least Effort in The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, where Chopra defines acceptance as agreeing to accept this moment as it is because struggling against it is struggling against the whole universe. I am confident in the book and chapter; I cannot verify the exact wording or page.

earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Intention and Desire chapter (page unverified)
notes: A well-known passage from the Law of Intention and Desire chapter; 'attention energizes, and intention transforms' and 'intention organizes its own fulfillment' are Chopra's exact formulations from that book. Strong attribution; I have not confirmed the page, so I am not claiming primary-source verification.

earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Dharma chapter (page unverified)
notes: This is essentially the opening statement of the Law of Dharma chapter, where Chopra states that everyone has a purpose and a unique talent, and that blending that talent with service to others is the goal of goals. Attribution and book are secure in my knowledge; the ellipsis suggests light editing from the original sentence.

The language is unmistakably Chopra's Vedanta framing — unity consciousness, the unified field, 'the seer and the scenery are one' — and it is consistently credited to him. I cannot place which book it comes from (candidates include The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success and Ageless Body, Timeless Mind), so I am not asserting a source.

One of the most widely circulated Denis Waitley lines, attributed to him uniformly across compilations and consistent with his Seeds of Greatness material. No primary source known to me, so the attribution is strong by repetition rather than by citation.

I have no knowledge of Denise Trifiletti or of this passage. The length and register suggest it was excerpted from a contributed essay in a multi-author inspirational anthology rather than being a circulating quotation. I cannot confirm or dispute the attribution — the honest answer here is that I do not know.

Attributed to Dhyani Ywahoo, the Cherokee teacher and author of Voices of Our Ancestors (1987), which would be the natural source. I recall the attribution but cannot confirm the passage in that book or any other, so the citation stays open.

Diana Hunt co-authored The Tao of Time (1990) with Pam Hait, and this line's theme of busyness as the measure of time fits that book, which is presumably why it is credited to her. I cannot verify the passage, and where a book has two authors an unattributed excerpt is doubly uncertain.

This is Demosthenes, not Diane Arbus. The line is a standard English rendering from the Third Olynthiac: 'Nothing is easier than self-deceit. For what each man wishes, that he also believes to be true.' It has nothing to do with photography and predates Arbus by well over two millennia. Confidence here reflects my certainty in the Demosthenes attribution. Note that this is one of three quotes in this batch wrongly filed under Arbus (see also q_0520 and q_0522), which suggests a block-assignment error in the upstream source list rather than three independent slips.

earliest_print_source: The Ascent of Man, Jacob Bronowski, 1973
notes: This is Jacob Bronowski from The Ascent of Man (1973), in the discussion of toolmaking and human evolution: 'The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.' Both sentences are his, not Diane Arbus's. Confidence reflects certainty in the Bronowski attribution; I have not verified the page. Second of three Arbus misfilings in this batch.

earliest_print_source: Diane Arbus: An Aperture Monograph, 1972 (drawn from her 1971 class transcripts; page unverified)
notes: Genuine Arbus. This comes from her own words as collected in the posthumous Aperture monograph, largely transcribed from the master class she taught in 1971. The 'I arrange myself' formulation is distinctively hers and is quoted consistently in Arbus scholarship. Holding just at the bar because I cannot confirm the page.

earliest_print_source: Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs, Thomas Fuller, 1732
notes: Not Diane Arbus. This is a proverb collected by Thomas Fuller in Gnomologia (1732), whose form is 'If you have knowledge, let others light their candles at it' (note 'at', not 'in'). It is also very commonly misattributed to Margaret Fuller, the 19th-century American writer, apparently through surname confusion. Confidence reflects my certainty that the line is the Fuller proverb rather than anything of Arbus's; between Thomas Fuller as collector and any earlier proverbial origin, Gnomologia is the earliest print appearance I know. Third of three Arbus misfilings in this batch.
suggested_reattribution: Thomas Fuller (Gnomologia, 1732); frequently misattributed to Margaret Fuller

earliest_print_source: Diane Arbus: An Aperture Monograph, 1972 (page unverified)
notes: Genuine and one of Arbus's most famous statements, quoted throughout photography criticism, including in discussions of her work by Susan Sontag and others. It appears among her own writings and class remarks collected in the Aperture monograph. Attribution is as solid as secondary evidence gets; I have not confirmed the page, so this stays below the primary-source band.

Diane Mariechild is a real author — Mother Wit (1981) and The Inner Dance — and this is credited to her in quote compilations, but I cannot locate it in her work or identify any earlier appearance. No traceable source; 'I don't know' is the honest verdict.
